title: The small things
hook: the Buddha refrains from even small unkindness, like idle talk and shows
carry: the ground the summit stands on

segments.voice: Yesterday: vanna and avanna, praise and blame on the road, and your line, not elated, not angry. Today, what people actually praise the Buddha for.

Board games on eight-row and ten-row boards. Games played on imaginary boards in the air. Dice. Toy plows and toy windmills. Guessing what a friend is thinking. Elephant fights, ballad singers, acrobats. This is a real list, from the first long discourse, a snapshot of what people did for fun long ago. It's there because the Buddha is describing what he doesn't do. These little things, he says, are what an ordinary person praises him for.
screen: `DICE, BOARD GAMES, ELEPHANT FIGHTS.` → `A SNAPSHOT OF ANCIENT FUN.` → `WHAT PEOPLE PRAISE HIM FOR.`

segments.voice: When an ordinary person praises me, he tells the monks, it's for small matters, mere moral conduct. Then he lists them. He's put down the stick and the sword. He's gentle and kind, compassionate toward all living beings. He takes only what's given. He speaks the truth; he's reliable. He doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them apart; he brings together those who are divided, and enjoys harmony. His speech isn't harsh. It's pleasant to the ear, it goes to the heart. He doesn't waste words, and speaks at the right time, about what's true and useful. Then the finer points. He doesn't damage seeds or plants. He doesn't go to shows: dancing, singing, music, those elephant fights. He doesn't play the games. He doesn't trade in false weights and measures. He doesn't pass the day in what the text calls low talk: kings and robbers, food and clothes, gossip at the well. The Pali word for all this is sila: moral conduct, virtue. And here's the twist. The Buddha calls it small. The real teaching is deeper, and the rest of the discourse goes there. But he practices every one of the small things anyway. They aren't the summit. They're the ground the summit stands on.
screen: `WHAT ORDINARY PEOPLE PRAISE` · `NO STICK, NO SWORD, NO TALE-BEARING` · `NO SHOWS, NO GAMES, NO LOW TALK` · `SMALL, BUT THE GROUND OF IT ALL` · then, large: `THE SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Go through the list slowly, gentle speech, no carrying tales, speaking at the right time, not wasting words, taking only what's given, and let the one closest to your actual life light up. Picture the moment it usually comes, see yourself meeting it with a little more care, then rest with the breath.
Sila. Moral conduct, virtue, in its smallest forms: kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. Small, and still practiced.
Your line: the ground the summit stands on. He called it small, and kept every piece. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and in Theravada communities some take eight on observance days, which add refraining from entertainments, adornment and luxurious beds: a lay echo of the conduct listed in DN 1.

original.note: Pali sila (Sanskrit shila): moral conduct, virtue, the ground of practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: small things don't matter much in a spiritual life.
what it means: the Buddha calls them small but practices every one, as the ground of everything else.
what a scholar hears: the morality sections (short, middle, long) recur in all thirteen opening discourses of the Digha, which is why the first division is called the Silakkhandha Vagga.

chat.says: If the Buddha called good conduct small, why bother with it?
options: He called it small beside deeper teaching, yet kept every bit: it's the ground.
Because it's all there is; he never taught anything deeper than manners.
Because people will praise you for it, and that praise is the real goal.
chat.meaning: The Buddha calls moral conduct a small matter next to the deeper teaching, yet practices all of it. It's the ground the summit stands on.
